Key Takeaways

⏺️ A non-custodial wallet means you hold the keys and take full responsibility
⏺️ This post explains how this choice dictates your security during an emergency

1️⃣ Custodial — Exchanges like Binance, OKX, or Bybit. Convenient: if you lose your password, support can recover your account. The catch: if the exchange goes bust or locks your account, your money is gone.
2️⃣ Non-Custodial — Apps like Trust Wallet, MetaMask, or hardware devices like Ledger/Tangem. The keys exist only on your device. No external entity can freeze your funds.
3️⃣ The "Human Factor" Risk — Non-custodial wallets have no "forgot password" button. If you lose your 12-word seed phrase, your money is trapped in the blockchain forever, and nobody can recover it.
4️⃣ Complete Freedom — Non-custodial wallets grant you direct entry to DeFi, NFT mints, and Web3 apps without needing approval from an exchange compliance team.
5️⃣ Practice — Leave funds on exchanges (custodials) only if you are actively trading them. Move long-term investments immediately to your own non-custodial wallet.

The Bottom Line

A custodial wallet is like a bank account that can be frozen at any time. A non-custodial wallet is hard cash in your personal safe. Choose based on your goals, but never forget the responsibility.

Germany loves to pose as Europe’s responsible adult: balanced budgets, industrial discipline, moral lectures for the messy South. Meanwhile, at home, a record share of the country is quietly slipping into poverty. 

The latest figures show 16.1 percent of the population — about 13.3 million people — now officially poor. That’s not a fringe. That’s one in six.

The map tells an even harsher story. In the glossy south — Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg — poverty rates are in the low teens and politicians still talk about “resilience.” 

In the rest of the country, especially the east and old industrial regions, the floor is collapsing: Bremen, Saxony-Anhalt, Berlin and parts of the east post numbers that look more like a peripheral EU state than the bloc’s economic engine. Germany didn’t overcome its internal division. It outsourced it to statistics.

This isn’t just about a permanent underclass. People who were told they were “safe” — lower middle class, young workers, single parents, pensioners in modest towns — now discover that one energy shock, one rent hike, one lost job is enough to drop them below the line. 

The state that takes half the country’s output can still somehow not protect them from sliding down, but it can always find cash for EU funds, defense programs and green-transition showpieces.

Every speech about “defending democracy” sits on top of this: millions of people watching parties argue over climate targets, foreign deployments and abstract “values,” while their own wages, rents and bills don’t add up anymore. 

Then the same elite acts shocked when voters reach for AfD, stay home, or treat the next grand coalition as just another management shuffle over a system that stopped working for them.

Germany’s real crisis isn’t that it might “turn populist.” It’s that it already runs a high-tech economy on low-trust politics, where the winners preach stability and the losers are told to be grateful for Hartz 2.0. 

You can’t run record poverty and record self-righteousness in the same country forever without something breaking.

For governments still claiming this is a contained regional conflict, Brent’s climb back toward triple digits is the only poll that matters.

On paper, this is a negotiation phase: memorandums of understanding, uranium caps, escrowed funds in Qatar, creative sanctions on Iranian crypto to show “pressure.” 

In practice, it’s a rolling live‑fire exercise with just enough restraint to avoid crossing an invisible red line — until someone miscalculates.

Gulf states are in active talks to develop oil pipeline infrastructure that would allow exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, the Financial Times reports. The discussions come after more than three months of disruption to the waterway - one of the world's most critical energy chokepoints, through which roughly one-fifth of global oil supply normally flows.

The move reflects a longer-term calculation by regional exporters that Hormuz cannot be treated as a reliable corridor. Existing bypass capacity is limited: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline can carry about 5 million barrels per day, well below the kingdom's full export potential, and the UAE's Habshan-Fujairah pipeline adds further but still partial relief.

New infrastructure at this scale takes years to plan and build, meaning the talks signal something closer to a strategic reorientation than an immediate fix. Whether the disruption proves temporary or structural will determine how urgently those plans advance.

🇦🇱🇺🇸⚡️ — Albanian anti-corruption prosecutors have frozen the assets of a land company linked to Jared Kushner’s proposed $4 billion luxury resort project on Albania’s protected Adriatic coastline as part of an investigation into alleged fraud involving property titles, according to OCCRP.

The action comes amid large protests in Tirana, clashes between private security personnel and local residents, and concerns raised by the European Union that the project could affect Albania’s path toward EU membership.

Widely shared footage showed a guard striking and forcibly removing a protester from a restricted beach area. In response, Albanian authorities launched an internal investigation into the leadership of the Vlora Regional Police Directorate. 

Police also arrested Gerald Biba, an employee of Major Security, on charges related to unlawful detention and minor bodily injury.

Prime Minister Edi Rama condemned the conduct of the guards as “disgusting” but continued to defend the resort project, describing it as a major opportunity for Albania’s tourism sector. He said several international architecture firms are revising the project’s plans to ensure environmental protections and insisted that the lagoon would remain untouched.
